title: MAGE: Towards Generalizable Multi-timescale EEG Representations
claim: A multi-part pipeline combines multi-scale tokenization, encoding, and adaptive aggregation, trained with dual losses, to capture signal structure at several resolutions.
layout: 3 modules, bottom-to-top flow, zoomed encoder inset at left, dashed boxes group stages
description: A dense block diagram where data flows bottom to top. At the bottom, raw multichannel EEG input and a masked copy feed two Multi-timescale Tokenization boxes (A), which produce grids of tokens at three granularities. The masked branch goes through a Multi-timescale Encoder and Predictor. The unmasked branch goes through an EMA-updated Target Encoder. Both sit in a gray Representation space box with an Alignment Loss. Predictor outputs go to a Multi-timescale Reconstructor, then to three multiplication nodes that merge them into a reconstructed EEG signal. A blue dashed Aggregator panel (C) uses temporal and spectral analysis plus an MLP to weight each scale. At the far left, a purple inset (B) zooms into the encoder, showing stacked LayerNorm, Temporal Attention, Spatial Attention and Feed-Forward blocks with residual connections. Pastel colors separate modules, and orange loss boxes sit at the top right.
caption: Overview of the MAGE pretraining pipeline. MAGE employs (A) Multi-timescale tokenization and (B) Multi-timescale encoder, optimized with a dual-loss scheme for both semantic and fine-grained learning. (C) Multi-timescale Aggregator dynamically weights each scale for the final reconstruction.
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) data plays an important role in understanding human brain activity, with various major applications. While current approaches, which largely build on EEG foundation models, have demonstrated strong performance across datasets and tasks, they typically rely on a fixed temporal scale. This design choice limits their ability to capture characteristics of neural dynamic behavior, often spanning across multiple timescales, which are naturally captured in EEG recordings. To address this limitation, we propose MAGE (\textbf{Multi-timescale Adaptive Generalization for EEG}), a foundation model that dynamically adapts to capture and integrate information across different timescales. Specifically, MAGE combines two key mechanisms: (i) a novel multi-timescale attention mechanism, capable of learning representations across multiple temporal scales and (ii) a trainable aggregation module, that dynamically identifies and adapts to the most informative timescale of the input signal. Experimental results across seven datasets demonstrate that MAGE consistently outperforms existing EEG foundation models while using substantially fewer parameters. Moreover, our results support the hypothesis that different downstream tasks benefit from distinct temporal scales.
